rv.q: It's an utterly disarming evening that shows happiness as a day-to-day mindset, not a far-off dream.
I've rarely been in a theatre where the spectators seemed to breathe so much in time with a show.

The come-one, come-all spirit of the new venue suits the daffy alchemy of an evening which starts like a potentially alienating in-joke and builds, by degrees and via an ingredient-spattering cooking session, to a shared delirium of life-affirming silliness.
This show is about joy, as much as difficulty, and it's refreshing to watch something that celebrates difference without falling into pat sentimentality.
Occasionally it becomes too determinedly playful; it could be stronger for being a little darker.
Like its subject, this playful, exuberant theatrical happening wins you over with sheer heart and good humour.
Its message of optimism and inclusivity is hard to resist – and makes a robustly positive mission statement for Burns' venture.
Michael Hugo's 'Nello' is perhaps even better than Toby Jones in the film, as he guides the other six actors through his life story.
For such an interesting man, this production feels like a slog.
'Marvellous' is one of the first times a West End show seemed to authentically present elements of neurodiversity in both casting and script, while never overly laden with sign-posting or preaching.
Its optimistic warmth makes Marvellous an audience-friendly opener for Nimax's new theatre.
The show is a list of actions which don't add up to a drama.
You really do need a sunny disposition to love, rather than just admire, this show.
